q: Block says functionalism replaces behaviorism's 'sensory inputs' with:
a: 'Sensory inputs and mental states', and 'disposition to act' with 'disposition to act and have certain mental states'
e: Functionalists individuate mental states partly by their causal relations to other mental states.

q: From the functionalist's point of view, behaviorism is guilty of:
a: Liberalism: ascribing mental properties to things that lack them
e: A system could have the right input-output relations without the right internal states.

q: From the functionalist's point of view, physicalism (pain = a brain state) is guilty of:
a: Chauvinism: withholding mental properties from systems that have them
e: It 'unfairly excludes those poor brainless creatures who nonetheless have minds'.

q: Block's two major theses are that functionalism is guilty of liberalism, and that:
a: Any version that avoids liberalism falls into chauvinism
e: So no version of functionalism can avoid both.

q: Why does Block say functionalism only 'tacks down' mental states at the periphery?
a: Its inputs and outputs are specified in physical/nonmental terms, while internal states are defined only by their roles
w: It only applies to the skin
It defines mental states by brain chemistry
e: This is why it inherits behaviorism's liberalism problem.

q: Block says the argument against physicalism isn't merely that one Turing machine can be made of wood, metal or glass, because:
a: That would be like arguing temperature can't be microphysical since different materials share it
w: Turing machines can only be made of silicon
e: The real point: it's hard to find any nontrivial physical property common to ALL possible realizations.

q: What's the difference between Functionalism and Psychofunctionalism?
a: Functionalism uses a common-sense psychological theory; Psychofunctionalism uses a scientific psychological theory
w: Psychofunctionalism is a form of dualism
e: Both identify mental states with their 'Ramsey functional correlates' relative to some theory.

q: In Lewis's version, mental terms are defined using a modification of whose method, eliminating mental vocabulary but keeping input/output terms?
a: Ramsey's
e: Replace the mental terms in a theory with variables and existentially quantify: the Ramsey sentence.

q: In the first homunculi-headed robot, little men inside the head each:
a: Implement one 'square' (quadruple) of your machine table, e.g., if card reads G and light I17 is on, press O191 and change card to M
e: Despite each man's low intelligence, the whole system realizes your functional organization.

q: In the China version, what replaces the bulletin board?
a: Letters displayed on satellites visible from anywhere in China
e: Each person gets a two-way radio connecting them to others and to the artificial body.

q: How does Block reply to the objection that a flood of the Yangtze could disrupt the Chinese system?
a: Whoever specifies the system decides what counts as inputs; a flood is like a bomb in a computer
e: Neural signals in Chungking residents no more count as inputs than tape jammed by a saboteur into a computer's relays.

q: Block's reply to 'the Chinese system would be too slow' involves imagining:
a: Beings we could only communicate with via time-lapse photography
e: Taking time scale as all-important 'seems crudely behavioristic'. Metaphysical possibility is all his argument needs.

q: When asked what qualia are, Block quotes:
a: Louis Armstrong on jazz: 'If you got to ask, you ain't never gonna get to know'
e: Qualitative states, 'raw feels', or what it's like (Nagel) to be the system.

q: The Absent Qualia Argument runs: machine functionalism says qualitative state Q = machine state Sq. But if there's nothing it's like to be the homunculi-head, then:
a: It can't be in Q even when in Sq, so there's prima facie doubt that Q = Sq
e: Block argues this intuition has a rational basis, not just raw intuition.

q: Putnam stipulated that no pain-feeler can decompose into parts that themselves have the relevant description. His aim was to rule out:
a: Swarms of bees as single pain-feelers
e: Block argues requiring NO sentient parts would wrongly exclude pregnant women and people with sentient parasites.

q: In the 'elementary-particle people' example, tiny beings pilot spaceships mimicking our particles, and you come to be made of their 'matter'. Block's verdict:
a: You'd still feel pain, since your synapses' electrochemical mechanisms are unchanged
e: So it isn't the parts' mentality per se that bothers us. It's how their mentality contributes to the whole.

q: What key difference between elementary-particle people and the original homunculi-heads explains our differing intuitions?
a: The particle-people change only your microphysics, not your psychology or neurophysiology
e: Our mental states plausibly depend on having the psychology and/or neurophysiology we have.

q: If no physical mechanism (not even a brain) seems intuitively like a seat of qualia, why may we disregard doubts about brain-headed systems but NOT homunculi-heads?
a: We know we are brain-headed and have qualia
e: This makes the argument partly empirical, but it's knowledge we actually have.

q: Why does Block say inference to the best explanation doesn't support homunculi-heads having pain?
a: The best explanation of their winces is that they were designed to mimic ours
e: We, by contrast, weren't designed to mimic anything.

q: Block's machine that stores all 'smart speakable strings' (sensible hour-long conversations) and looks up replies shows that:
a: A system could pass the Turing Test with no mental states at all (just a list-searcher plus tape recorder)
w: The Turing Test is a perfect test of mind
e: Taking complex behavior as sufficient for qualia 'is just crude behaviorism'.

q: 'The horse raced past the barn fell' is used by Block to make what point?
a: Intuitions can be overridden by theory: the sentence feels ungrammatical but is grammatical
e: Intuitions unsupported by principle aren't bedrock. Yet Block argues his anti-homunculi intuition IS supported.

q: Block notes each homunculus could be provably replaced by:
a: A McCulloch-Pitts 'and' neuron: two inputs, fires only if both receive a signal
e: So the argument doesn't depend on the homunculi's own mentality at all.
